title: The Pyramid Builder's Logbook
voice_direction: Measured, warm documentary storyteller with a quiet sense of wonder; crisp, confident hook; unhurried through the logbook details; a level, careful tone on the slaves question; the last line dry and soft, with a small pause before 'the paperwork'.
narration: The oldest written papyrus is a pyramid builder's logbook. Found in two thousand thirteen, at an old harbour on the Red Sea. Its author, an inspector named Merer, ran a crew of boatmen for King Khufu. Their cargo: white limestone from Tura, sailed down the Nile to Giza, probably for the Great Pyramid's outer casing. Two or three round trips every ten days, logged in half-day steps: where they sailed, what they carried, where they slept. [pause] Other pages tracked food and supplies for his men. The old story says slaves built the pyramids. This diary can't settle that. But a workers' town and tombs at Giza point one way: organised crews, fed by the state. Probably not slaves. Not exactly volunteers, either. The king left the pyramid. [pause] The crew left the paperwork.

instagram_caption:
In 2013, archaeologists led by Pierre Tallet found rolls of papyrus at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on Egypt's Red Sea coast. They are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found, from near the end of King Khufu's reign, about 2560 BC.

Several belong to an inspector named Merer, who ran a crew of boatmen. His logbook follows them loading white limestone at the Tura quarries and sailing it down the Nile to Giza, most likely for the Great Pyramid's smooth outer casing.

He wrote it all down in half-day steps: two or three round trips every ten days, where they sailed, what they carried, where they spent the night. He reported to Ankhhaf, the king's half-brother. Other sheets account for food and supplies for his men.

The diary alone can't tell us whether these men were free. But the workers' town and the builders' tombs excavated at Giza point the same way: organised, rotating crews, fed by the state. Probably not the slaves of legend, though not exactly volunteers either.

The king left the pyramid. The crew left the paperwork.

facts.claim: The Wadi al-Jarf papyri, including Merer's logbook, are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found (older blank rolls exist, so the script says 'written')
facts.source: Guinness World Records, 'Oldest papyrus'; Egyptian Ministry of Antiquities via Times of Israel (July 2016); Smithsonian Magazine, A. Stille, 'The World's Oldest Papyrus and What It Can Tell Us About the Great Pyramids' (2015)

facts.claim: Found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on the Red Sea coast, by the mission of Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard (with Sayed Mahfouz); the first batch on 24 March 2013 near storage gallery G2
facts.source: Times of Israel (July 2016, ministry statement); National Geographic, Red Sea Scrolls excerpt (Tallet & Lehner, The Red Sea Scrolls, Thames & Hudson 2021)

facts.claim: The author identifies himself as Inspector Merer; he led a team shipping limestone from Tura to Giza
Dated to 'the year after the 13th cattle count' of Khufu, i.e. year 26 or 27, near the end of his reign, c. 2560 BC
facts.source: Times of Israel / Egyptian ministry (2016); Smithsonian Magazine (c. 2560 BCE, last known year of Khufu); Guinness ('last years of Khufu's reign, probably around 2570 BCE')

facts.claim: Limestone from Tura sailed down the Nile to Giza, probably for the Great Pyramid's outer casing
facts.source: Smithsonian Magazine (2015: 'the builders finishing the pyramid's outer casing'); Tallet as summarised in Wikipedia 'Diary of Merer' / 'Ankhhaf' ('Tallet believes the operations refer to the delivery of the Tura limestone used for the casing')

facts.claim: Two or three round trips between Tura and Giza per ten-day Egyptian week (flood season)
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Diary of Merer', summarising Tallet, Les papyrus de la mer Rouge I (2017)

facts.claim: Merer reported to Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, who ran the harbour centre Ro-She Khufu
Merer logged his time in half-day increments: sailing, loading stone, and where the crew spent the night
facts.source: Smithsonian Magazine (2015); log entries as translated in Wikipedia 'Diary of Merer' (paraphrased, not quoted, in the script)

facts.claim: Separate sheets account for food and other supplies for the crew
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Diary of Merer' (summary of Tallet); Tallet & Marouard 2014 (Near Eastern Archaeology) cited in Belmonte/Magli arXiv 2411.08061 for food delivered to a team of workers

facts.claim: The slave-built pyramid is a popular myth; tombs of pyramid builders beside the pyramids (announced 2010 by Zahi Hawass) are taken as evidence the builders were not slaves
facts.source: AP via NBC News, 'Egypt discovers workers' tombs near pyramids' (Jan 2010); CBC (Jan 2010)

facts.claim: Mark Lehner's excavation of the workers' town (Heit el-Ghurab) since 1988 found bakeries, granaries and cattle bones; rotating crews passed through during periods of obligatory labour (hence 'not exactly volunteers')
facts.source: AERA, 'Dr. Mark Lehner'; Syracuse University News, Lehner Phanstiel lecture (Nov 2024); RAWI, 'Feeding the Forces'

facts.claim: The papyri were shown to the public for the first time at the Egyptian Museum, Cairo, in July 2016
facts.source: Times of Israel (July 2016); Mada Masr, 'Egypt's oldest papyrus on display, details construction of Great Pyramid'

diagram_notes.egypt_map: Schematic map of northern Egypt on cream paper: the Nile running north into the Delta; Giza on the west bank (small pyramid glyph, 'akhet-khufu · giza'); the Tura quarries just upstream on the east bank ('tura · limestone'); a dashed boat route Tura -> Giza drawn on as the beat plays; to the east the Gulf of Suez / Red Sea with Wadi al-Jarf marked by a pulsing dot ('wadi al-jarf · papyri found 2013'). Labelled 'schematic · drawn for this video · not to scale'.
diagram_notes.logbook_days: Dark panel: a strip of ten day-columns ('day 1' ... 'day 10', one Egyptian ten-day week), each split into two half-day cells (am / pm), filling in one by one with small icons: load stone at tura, sail downriver, overnight at she-khufu (moon), arrive akhet-khufu (pyramid), sail back upriver. Ink-brown strokes on papyrus-coloured cells. Labelled 'illustration · drawn for this video · not a transcription of the papyrus'.
